Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

The resulting type‑mismatch caused the C compiler to reject builds of Cython code that calls this iterator routine; updating the declaration eliminates those errors.

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: The apparent memory accumulation in the traced MPS workload is explained by the combination of deferred command buffer commitment (COMMIT_ADAPTIVE) and Python's garbage collection timing. Each iteration allocates a new output tensor that stays alive until no references remain — even if the result isn't assigned. Since the GPU doesn't immediately free buffers unless forced, the memory footprint appears to grow linearly. This is correct behavior under the current model; however, users may misinterpret it as a leak without understanding the decoupling between CPU-side object lifecycle and GPU-side resource management.

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Reference to device-specific behavior, as memory watermark triggers for adaptive commit may vary across hardware.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement: numpy.mean invokes the object's 'mean' attribute and forwards the 'axis' keyword argument, as shown by the TypeError when the attribute is set to None or a lambda function.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: According to the NCCL development team, the historical behavior of ncclCommGetAsyncError was that of a read‑only query; while the API never explicitly guaranteed read‑only semantics, the underlying code up to version 2.25 never performed any side‑effects. In the 2.26 release we made a targeted change to eliminate a race condition that could occur during the cleanup phase of asynchronous operations launched by non‑blocking communicators. The modification adds a small amount of cleanup work to the function, so that invoking ncclCommGetAsyncError now both fetches the current error status and may tidy up lingering asynchronous state. This resolves the concurrency issue but also means the function is no longer a pure read operation as it once was.

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: The interaction between MPS command buffer management and Python garbage collection may affect perceived memory usage patterns in user code.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Linking to the SciPy effort on extending multivariate distributions and aligning them with NumPy's behavior.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s

Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: A modified script that allows adaptive commits to complete demonstrates that memory is freed after approximately 5–6 seconds of waiting, consistent with the observed garbage‑collection behavior.

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: I’m confident that the memory behavior you’re seeing is expected: each iteration allocates a linear‑layer output of size 4 × N × C × H × W bytes, and with COMMIT_ADAPTIVE the MPS command buffer accumulates operations without committing until the device’s low‑memory watermark is reached. This keeps the output tensors alive until the Python objects are garbage‑collected. Switching to COMMIT_AND_WAIT forces immediate commits and releases the buffers as soon as the computation finishes, which is why you observe the memory being freed promptly. My tests show a ~5‑6 second delay for cleanup on a local setup, but actual workloads will experience variable delays depending on additional synchronization calls. The system is managing memory correctly; the adaptive commit mode simply obscures when the releases happen.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: The behavior of ncclCommGetAsyncError changed in NCCL 2.26 to fix a subtle race during async op cleanup. Before that, it was a read-only function by accident — not design. Now, when invoked, it may also clean up internal resources tied to completed or failed operations, especially in nonblocking contexts. So if you’re relying on it being side-effect-free, that assumption no longer holds.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: NCCL 2.26 redefined ncclCommGetAsyncError to include light cleanup logic during error polling — a change motivated by the need to fix race conditions in nonblocking communicator teardown. This is not a deviation from spec, but a correction of an undocumented implementation artifact that had been relied upon de facto.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: From the NCCL team's notes: before NCCL 2.26, ncclCommGetAsyncError acted as a read‑only operation; post‑2.26 it may also run a small cleanup step.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: From the NCCL team's standpoint, ncclCommGetAsyncError was historically a read-only function — it merely polled the async error state without side effects, though this was never part of the contract. This changed in NCCL 2.26 to address a race condition during cleanup of nonblocking communicator operations; now, under certain conditions, it triggers minimal internal cleanup to ensure safe state transition, making it no longer strictly idempotent.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Thanks for hanging in there, @hvaara – my deep dive into the metal‑resource logs suggests that each iteration expands the memory by about 4 × N × C × H × W bytes, which corresponds to the Linear layer's output allocated at line 50. When `executeMPSGraph` is invoked with `SyncMode::COMMIT_ADAPTIVE`, the operation is recorded into the active MPSStream command buffer, but unless the device's memory pressure exceeds a certain low‑watermark, the buffer remains uncommitted, causing subsequent iterations to pile onto the same buffer. Since each `nn.Linear` call retains its output tensor until the Python reference is cleared, the resident memory climbs while the command buffer accumulates more encoded ops. Using `COMMIT_AND_WAIT` forces a commit after each encode, which should free the output buffers once the call completes, likely giving the Python garbage collector a chance to reclaim the tensors (we never assign the results). I verified this by allowing the adaptive commit to run its course and then sleeping for roughly 5‑6 seconds, after which the memory usage dropped. In production, other synchronizations would trigger similar reclamation. Therefore, my tentative conclusion is that the observed memory pattern is by design; the opacity of `COMMIT_ADAPTIVE` stems from its device‑dependent commit policy and the timing of Python‑level deallocation. Let me know if this interpretation aligns with your experience or if additional investigation is needed.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.

It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. original_statement: This PR fixes a type mismatch in the Cython declarations for the NpyIter_GetIterNext function. The function was incorrectly declared to return NpyIter_IterNextFunc* (pointer to function type) when it should return NpyIter_IterNextFunc (function type directly). This mismatch causes compilation errors when users try to build Cython code that uses this function.
rephrased_statement: This pull request addresses a bug in the Cython definitions for `NpyIter_GetIterNext`. The wrapper mistakenly said the function returns a `NpyIter_IterNextFunc*` (a pointer), yet the actual NumPy C API returns a `NpyIter_IterNextFunc` (the callable type). Because Cython trusts the declaration, it produced mismatched code and developers saw compilation errors when importing the function. By correcting the return type to the proper function type, we get rid of those errors and ensure the iterator’s next‑function can be used seamlessly in Cython modules.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Switching SyncMode to COMMIT_AND_WAIT results in immediate command buffer commitment and earlier release of associated memory buffers after computation completion.

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1

    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations.     When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Hey @hvaara, appreciate the patience! After tracing the metal allocations I’ve pieced together a likely explanation: every iteration allocates an output tensor for the linear layer (about 4 × N × C × H × W bytes) at L50, so memory grows linearly; with COMMIT_ADAPTIVE the commands just keep getting queued in the same MPSStream buffer until the GPU gets low on memory, meaning the buffer isn’t flushed immediately; each nn.Linear output lives until Python’s GC can collect it, which explains the steady memory climb while the command buffer accumulates work. If we flip to COMMIT_AND_WAIT, each encode is committed right away and the output buffers get freed once the call returns – the GC then sees no references and cleans up. I added a small delay (≈5‑6 s) to let the adaptive commit finish and saw the memory drop. So it seems the system is behaving as designed, though COMMIT_ADAPTIVE can look flaky because its commit timing depends on device‑specific memory thresholds and GC timing. Let me know if that matches your observations or if you’ve run into a concrete problem.

 import torch
 torch.random.manual_seed(42)
 from torch import nn
 

 dtype = torch.float16
 batch, seq, embed_dim, delay = 2, 16, 4, 2
 x1 = torch.randn(batch, seq, embed_dim, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
 x2 = x1[:, delay:]

 out1 = net(x1)
 out2 = net(x2)
 print((out1[:, delay:] - out2).abs().max())
 assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)

 tensor(0.0010, device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.float16, grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 Traceback (most recent call last):

  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.

 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s

 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.

Let me give you some background on this issue from the NCCL team's perspective:
 Until recently, ncclCommGetAsyncError was, as @ptrblck said, a pure read-op. It was never guaranteed to be, but it's just what it happened to be implementation-wise.
 This changed in NCCL 2.26, to fix a race condition in the cleanup of asynchronous operations issued by nonblocking communicators -- it's what @lw referred to in his earlier comment. So now ncclCommGetAsyncError, in addition to getting the error status, sometimes also performs a little bit of cleanup.
rephrased_statement: According to the NCCL team, ncclCommGetAsyncError was originally a read‑only call, not because of a spec guarantee but because that’s how it was coded before the recent changes.

original_statement:
Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: The root cause of apparent memory bloat is the decoupling of Python GC from Metal resource lifecycle under COMMIT_ADAPTIVE. Output tensors remain allocated until the MPS stream flushes, which occurs non-deterministically. This is intentional for performance — only use COMMIT_AND_WAIT if you need deterministic memory bounds.

original_statement: The error is referring to the fact that float(1).exp() fails. NumPy does not go to much effort to handle functions on object arrays. In general object arrays will never really be fully integrated into NumPy, and maybe were a mistake in the first place, but are convenient for some container-like applications. Object dtypes are "out of scope" for the Array API standard (point 4).
rephrased_statement: The traceback is basically saying ‘I can’t do `float(1).exp()` because the value is in an object array’. NumPy doesn’t try to support ufuncs on object‑dtype arrays – they’re a legacy feature used when you need a container for arbitrary Python objects, not a numeric computation engine. Because of that, the Array API standard explicitly excludes object dtypes (point 4), so you shouldn’t expect `.exp()` to work on them. The error is therefore the expected behavior.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)

>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.
rephrased_statement: Under COMMIT_ADAPTIVE, Metal retains output buffers across iterations because no explicit sync occurs. Memory pressure triggers batched commits, causing delayed GC of Python tensor refs. This isn't a bug — it's a performance optimization. If your app needs bounded memory, switch to COMMIT_AND_WAIT or explicitly del output + torch.mps.synchronize().

Ok @hvaara thanks for your patience! Here's the results from my deep dive to the traces of metal resources getting generated during the execution of the code snippet and my current understanding on what's going on:

    The memory grows by the size of the output object of linear layer for each iteration run so by 4 * N * C * H * W bytes, making sense since this is the output object we allocate on L50 in the linear op 1
    When the executeMPSGraph is called using COMMIT_ADAPTIVE as the SyncMode, the operation is encoded to the active command buffer in MPSStream but unless the memory pressure is too high, the command buffer is not committed but instead we keep on encoding operations to the same command buffer 2
    Since each iteration with the nn.Linear needs to maintain its own output tensor until the computation is completed and the python object goes out of scope to be garbage collected, we see the memory increase while the command buffer keeps accumulating more encoded operations. In case we change to COMMIT_AND_WAIT as our SyncMode the command buffers get committed after each encode and the memory buffers required for the outputs are also released once the computation returns. This probably lets the garbage collector sees that the object is no longer needed since we don't assign the outputs of the computation to anything in the python script.
    To validate this I tried to adjust the original script slightly to allow for the adaptive commit to run its course and the computations to return so that the underlying objects can be released and we can see the memory get freed up. It seems like on my local setup it takes about 5-6s of waiting for the objects to get cleaned up. In actual code I assume this would happen more often since there can be other operations calling the command buffer to get synchronized in between in order to perform updates based on the results.

So in summary to me it seems like the memory is managed as intended in this case. In its current form the COMMIT_ADAPTIVE is a bit opaque to the user since it might make the memory seem like its behaving erratically as the commit is automated to only happen once the local device hits the low memory watermark, which depends on the device you are running on. Additionally there's the interplay of when will the underlying python objects get garbage collected that should finally release the memory buffers assigned to them. Let me know if this sounds reasonable or if you think there's still something we missed here. Or if this is causing a concrete issue on your side that would warrant us to do some changes on how the adaptive commit works at the moment.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Documenting the interaction between the `size` argument and broadcasting of parameters for distributions like Dirichlet, Multinomial, and Multivariate Normal.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement: Seen a similar pattern with a `polars.Series` object: `np.mean(a)` raises `TypeError` because `Series.mean()` does not accept the `axis` keyword argument, while `np.mean(np.asarray(a))` works as expected.
