This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Output shape of rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2)) is observed as (10, 4, 2, 3), with components corresponding to size, broadcast shape, and variate dimension.

original_statement:
Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: Tagging @pytorch-macos-team for visibility on MPS performance characteristics.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])

  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Quick update on the SciPy multivariate distribution revamp: we want any new features or fixes to stay compatible with NumPy's existing and future multivariate distribution behavior. The main puzzle is how the `size` keyword works together with broadcasting when the distribution's parameters are supplied as arrays (some 1‑D, some 2‑D) rather than plain scalars. I'm mapping out the gufunc signatures for each distribution – for instance, `dirichlet` uses `(n) -> (n)` and `multinomial` uses `(),(n) -> (n)` – to see how the broadcasting should behave. @bashtage's PR gives us a nice example for `multinomial`, where you can pass a vector of `n` values and a matrix of `pvals` and get a nicely shaped output. Now we need to figure out how to apply that same broadcasting logic to the other multivariate methods so that `size` only controls the number of draws and not the internal variate dimensions.

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.

Thinking a bit more about this, I wonder if URI should statically allow us to register a scheme to behave like a file scheme. Because, we do take an existing well defined URI of scheme file and turn that into vscode-userdata. This in turn means, every client that deals with such a URI would need to ensure that the scheme is converted back to file before using the URI. That seems fragile.

If we could tell URI to treat vscode-userdata like a file scheme, maybe the change would be easier and less fragile?

 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Request to document or clarify expected behavior of size parameter across multivariate distribution methods in NumPy.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement: I'm not certain whether the presence of a .mean attribute on a foreign class triggers NumPy's internal dispatch mechanism, which appears to treat the attribute as if it were numpy.mean, leading to unexpected TypeError exceptions.

Because, we do take an existing well defined URI of scheme file and turn that into vscode-userdata. This in turn means, every client that deals with such a URI would need to ensure that the scheme is converted back to file before using the URI. That seems fragile.

If we could tell URI to treat vscode-userdata like a file scheme, maybe the change would be easier and less fragile?

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: I am uncertain whether the MPS slowdown is a symptom of missing ANE acceleration, as the CMake configuration selected Accelerate.framework but showed no power consumption from the ANE module, or whether the issue lies elsewhere in the PyTorch‑MPS integration; the same inference script runs in 36 s on MPS, 18 s on CPU, and 0.82 s on CUDA, despite full GPU utilization during the test.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Open question on how size parameter broadcasting behavior in multinomial should be aligned with other multivariate distributions.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)
rephrased_statement: I discovered today that numpy.mean() doesn't just look for array-like objects — it aggressively inspects any object for a .mean attribute and tries to call it with axis, dtype, etc. arguments. I didn't know this was a thing, and it broke my code when a third-party library added a .mean property to a class. I thought NumPy would coerce to array first — now I'm not sure what's safe to pass in. Is this a feature or a bug?

multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: As we refactor SciPy's multivariate distribution layer, I'm wondering whether the interaction between the `size` argument and gufunc‑style broadcasting (e.g., `mean` → (n), `cov` → (n,n)) can be made to mirror NumPy's current behavior without breaking future extensions.

Thank you so much for the detailed and insightful analysis.

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

torch.backends.cudnn.version() == 90100

This further supports the hypothesis that some low-level dispatch or fusion within cuDNN is not being properly marked as opaque or guarded during export tracing?

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This confirms that the problem is not limited to LSTM, but more broadly affects cuDNN-backed recurrent layers, including nn.RNN. Disabling torch.backends.cudnn.enabled continues to serve as a valid workaround in both cases.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: My benchmark shows MPS taking 36s vs CPU’s 18s for BERT with batch 64—even though the GPU is clearly active. I’ve read about 5x speedups on Hugging Face’s blog, so I’m wondering: is this a bug, a known limitation, or am I missing a critical setup step (like quantization or memory pinning)?

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

m = torch.compile(self.transformer.forward, fullgraph=True, dynamic=True, mode="max-autotune", disable=False)

m(...)

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: I don't know if it's a bug or a design choice that size in multivariate distributions omits the variate dimension from its shape — like in multivariate_normal where (n,) and (n,n) inputs with size=(5,) yield shape (5,n), not (5,n,n). Should we document this as intentional, or is this an inconsistency we should fix?

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.

 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s

 CUDA 0.82 s

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: How should we interpret `size` in NumPy’s multivariate distributions when parameters broadcast across multiple dimensions? For instance, `rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))` yields shape `(10, 4, 2, 3)`. Is the final `3` always the event dimension (fixed per distribution), and `size` only controls the *batch* shape? We need to know if this is an official contract or just current behavior.

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)

>>> import numpy as np

  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)

Traceback (most recent call last):

  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Hey folks, as part of the ongoing SciPy effort to polish up our multivariate distributions and roll out a few new ones, we need to double‑check that any changes we make stay in step with NumPy's current and upcoming multivariate distribution API. The sticking point right now is the `size` argument: it seems to get tangled up with broadcasting when the distribution parameters are arrays (think 1‑D or 2‑D) instead of simple scalars. To get a handle on this, I'm looking at the gufunc‑style signatures for each distribution – e.g., `multivariate_normal` is `(n),(n,n) -> (n)` – even though they're not actual gufuncs yet. The PR by @bashtage adds broadcasting support to `multinomial`, letting you do something like `rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10,4,2))` and get an output shape of `(10,4,2,3)`. The challenge now is to extend that broadcasting behavior to the other multivariate distribution functions so that `size` cleanly specifies the number of samples without accidentally adding extra dimensions from the parameter shapes.

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: We’re aligning SciPy’s new multivariate distribution implementations with NumPy’s evolving broadcasting rules. The `multinomial` PR demonstrates that `size` governs sample batch dimensions while leaving event dimensions (like the 3 in `(n)`) untouched. We’re uncertain whether all distributions should treat `size` identically, or if we need to account for differences in parameter structure (e.g., scalar `nsample` vs. vector `alpha`). Is this a design choice we’re free to make—or is there a hidden convention we’re missing?

Thinking a bit more about this, I wonder if URI should statically allow us to register a scheme to behave like a file scheme. Because, we do take an existing well defined URI of scheme file and turn that into vscode-userdata. This in turn means, every client that deals with such a URI would need to ensure that the scheme is converted back to file before using the URI. That seems fragile.

If we could tell URI to treat vscode-userdata like a file scheme, maybe the change would be easier and less fragile?
rephrased_statement: After further reflection, I’m wondering if the URI framework could be extended to let us declare a custom scheme that behaves identically to the built‑in `file` scheme. The current approach grabs a valid `file:` URI, rewrites it into a `vscode‑userdata:` URI, and then distributes that new URI to the rest of the code. Because of this, every component that receives the `vscode‑userdata` URI has to remember to translate it back to a `file:` URI before it can perform any file‑system operation, which feels like a delicate and error‑prone requirement. If the URI layer could be instructed to treat `vscode‑userdata` as a file‑scheme alias, we could eliminate the manual conversion step, potentially making the modification simpler, more robust, and less likely to break due to overlooked scheme handling.

  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.

original_statement:
Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: I thought MPS would speed up BERT inference on my MacBook, but it’s actually slower than the CPU. I even validated that the tensor operations are hitting the GPU—power usage, metrics, everything checks out. But performance is half of CPU. Is this a fundamental limitation of the Metal backend for NLP? Or is this something that’ll improve in PyTorch 2.4+?

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.
rephrased_statement: I’ve followed the recommended practices for MPS inference with Hugging Face BERT: using no_grad(), batch size 64, and confirmed hardware utilization. Yet performance is worse than CPU. I'm not sure whether this is an artifact of the Metal Performance Shaders library's current support for dynamic shapes in attention layers, or if there's an unrecognized overhead from converting between CoreML and PyTorch tensor formats. Has anyone else observed this bottleneck? Is it expected for early-stage MPS transformers?

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)

np.float64(1.0)

Using MPS for BERT inference appears to produce about a 2x slowdown compared to the CPU. Here is code to reproduce the issue:
 # MPS Version
 from transformers import AutoTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
 import timeit
 import torch
 

 tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased")
 model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("bert-base-cased").to(torch.device("mps"))
 

 tokens = tokenizer.tokenize("Hello world, this is michael!")
 tids = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids(tokens)
 with torch.no_grad():
  t_tids = torch.tensor([tids]*64, device=torch.device("mps"))
  res = timeit.timeit(lambda: model(input_ids=t_tids), number=100)
 print(res)
 

 torch.backends.mps.is_available() reports True as expected.
 I chose a batch size of 64, since that was mentioned on the blog post for the ~5x speedup in Huggingface BERT.
 Running this benchmark, swapping "mps" and "cpu" for the devices, I get:
 CPU 18.38 s
 MPS 36.00 s
 And, for comparison, running this same snippet on an A10G using CUDA 11.6 on an AWS g5.xlarge instance (ubuntu 20.04, pytorch 1.11.0 compiled from source), I get:
 CUDA 0.82 s
 I used the no_grad() construction due to the comment mentioned on #77753.
 I used today's nightly build. Furthermore, I also built PyTorch from source and observed no differences on the results here. Lastly, I confirmed with Activity Monitor and powermetrics that the GPU is in fact being used, seeing GPU usage at 98.8%, GPU power spike to 15711 mW when running the MPS benchmark, and CPU power spiking as expected when running the CPU benchmark.
 So it does seem like things are "hooked up" right, just not efficient.
 As a side note, when building PyTorch from source, I observed in the CMake logs that Accelerate.framework was selected as the BLAS library, but sadly I didn't observe any power consumption by the ANE module, which is too bad.

I’ve built PyTorch from source, confirmed no_grad(), and checked memory layout. The performance gap suggests that either the Metal backend lacks optimized kernels for transformer layers, or there’s a dispatch overhead in bridging Hugging Face’s model graph to MPS. Has anyone else observed this for BERT specifically? Is there a workaround to force kernel fusion or use a different attention implementation?

original_statement:
This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: Hey team, we're working on updating SciPy's multivariate distributions and want to be sure any changes still line up with NumPy's behavior. I'm not sure how the `size` argument interacts with broadcasting when some parameters are 1‑D or 2‑D arrays instead of scalars.

I accidentally discovered that nn.Linear with datatype float16/bfloat16 can produce significant numerical errors on sliced tensors:
 import torch
 torch.random.manual_seed(42)
 from torch import nn
 

 dtype = torch.float16
 batch, seq, embed_dim, delay = 2, 16, 4, 2
 x1 = torch.randn(batch, seq, embed_dim, device="cuda", dtype=dtype)
 x2 = x1[:, delay:]
 assert torch.allclose(x1[:, delay:], x2)
 net = nn.Linear(embed_dim, embed_dim).to("cuda").to(dtype=dtype)
 out1 = net(x1)
 out2 = net(x2)
 print((out1[:, delay:] - out2).abs().max())
 assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 

 I got the output like this:
 tensor(0.0010, device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.float16, grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 AssertionError
 

 If the type is bfloat16, the error is even greater:
 tensor(0.0078, device='cuda:0', dtype=torch.bfloat16, grad_fn=<MaxBackward1>)
 Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/jewel/Workspaces/cusrl/test.py", line 14, in <module>
  assert torch.allclose(out1[:, delay:], out2)
 AssertionError
 

 However, if the tensor is cloned after sliced x2 = x1[:, delay:].clone() or the type is float32, it will produce an error of exactly zero.

Thank you so much for the detailed and insightful analysis.

I followed your suggestion and tested with:

torch.backends.cudnn.enabled = False

As you anticipated, export on GPU succeeded when disabling cuDNN. This strongly indicates that the issue is indeed related to certain cuDNN-optimized fused kernels, likely being incorrectly traced during export when fake tensors are used.

For completeness, my environment reports the following cuDNN version:

torch.backends.cudnn.version() == 90100

This further supports the hypothesis that some low-level dispatch or fusion within cuDNN is not being properly marked as opaque or guarded during export tracing?

Additionally, I’d like to report that the same issue also occurs when using nn.RNN instead of nn.LSTM. Specifically, like:

self.rnn = nn.RNN(input_size, hidden_size, num_layers, batch_first=True)

This confirms that the problem is not limited to LSTM, but more broadly affects cuDNN-backed recurrent layers, including nn.RNN. Disabling torch.backends.cudnn.enabled continues to serve as a valid workaround in both cases.
rephrased_statement: The export issue was reproduced using nn.RNN with batch_first=True, in addition to nn.LSTM, indicating possible broader scope across cuDNN-backed recurrent layers.

Since there is a well defined interoperability protocol I was assuming that it is safe to call numpy functions on foreign objects, until I discovered this strange behaviour:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> class Kls: pass
...
>>> a = Kls()
>>> a.mean = None
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable
>>> a.mean = lambda : 0
>>> np.mean(a)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: <lambda>() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'

So if np.mean(a) discovers that a has a mean attribute, it blindly assumes that it is a method with the same semantics and signature of np.mean.

This is crazy! numpy does not owns the mean method and in fact other libraries implemented it in different ways:

>>> import polars as pl
>>> a = pl.Series([0, 1, 2])
>>> np.mean(a) #broken
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "/Users/miccoli/work/uvenv/bigdata/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/numpy/_core/fromnumeric.py", line 3858, in mean
    return mean(axis=axis, dtype=dtype, out=out, **kwargs)
           ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
TypeError: Series.mean() got an unexpected keyword argument 'axis'
>>> np.mean(np.asarray(a)) #works
np.float64(1.0)

Thinking a bit more about this, I wonder if URI should statically allow us to register a scheme to behave like a file scheme. Because, we do take an existing well defined URI of scheme file and turn that into vscode-userdata. This in turn means, every client that deals with such a URI would need to ensure that the scheme is converted back to file before using the URI. That seems fragile.

If we could tell URI to treat vscode-userdata like a file scheme, maybe the change would be easier and less fragile?

This issue is motivated by ongoing work in SciPy to improve the existing multivariate distributions and add new ones. We'd like to be sure that, if possible, enhancements that we make remain consistent with the current and future behavior of NumPy's multivariate distributions.

The specific issue is how the size parameter interacts with broadcasting of the distribution parameters, some of which are 1-d or 2-d arrays rather than scalars.

I'm going to refer to gufunc broadcasting, so it will be helpful to have the gufunc signatures of the existing multivariate distributions (even though they are not actually implemented as gufuncs):

Name                         Parameters      Gufunc signature
---------------------------  --------------  ----------------
dirichlet                    alpha           (n)       -> (n)
multinomial                  n, pvals        (),(n)    -> (n)
multivariate_normal          mean, cov       (n),(n,n) -> (n)
multivariate_hypergeometric  colors, nsample (n),()    -> (n)

@bashtage has a pull request to add broadcasting to multinomial. As an example, suppose I have four values of n, say 2, 5, 10 and 20, and I have two discrete probability distributions of length 3, say [0.1, 0.2, 0.7] and [0.8, 0.2, 0.0], and I want to generate 10 multinomial variates for each combination of those inputs. With the code in @bashtage's PR, we can write:

In [85]: n = np.array([2, 5, 10, 20]).reshape(-1, 1)

In [86]: pvals = np.array([[0.1, 0.2, 0.7], [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]])

In [87]: rng = np.random.default_rng()

In [88]: x = rng.multinomial(n, pvals, size=(10, 4, 2))

In [89]: x.shape
Out[89]: (10, 4, 2, 3)

The shape of the output has three sources: (10,) is the number of variates that we wanted for each combination of input parameters; (4, 2) is the broadcast shape of the input parameters, without the dimension associated with the gufunc signature; (3,) is the dimension associated with each variate.

Note that size is not the shape of the output array--size does not include the dimension associated with the variates themselves.

The question is how to adapt this to the other multivariate distribution methods.
rephrased_statement: For consistency across SciPy and NumPy, we need to understand the semantics of `size` when broadcasting 1D/2D parameters in multivariate distributions. For example, in `multinomial`, `size=(10, 4, 2)` with broadcastable `n` and `pvals` results in a final shape that includes the variate dimension (3). But does this apply uniformly to `multivariate_normal`? We’re unsure if this is a rule we must follow, or if it’s an inconsistency we should resolve—so we’re seeking guidance before proceeding.
